object_types.name: Customer
object_types.definition: A person or organization that places orders in the system. Identified by a unique customer ID in the CRM system.

source_references.excerpt: A customer places an order... Each customer has a unique customer ID in the CRM system.
I've heard some people call customers 'clients' in the billing system. Are those the same thing?... In our CRM they're 'customers' but the billing team calls them 'clients.'

object_types.name: Order

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: An item that can be ordered. Each product is identified by a unique SKU (stock-keeping unit code).

ambiguities.description: Customer name optionality is ambiguous. The transcript states 'every customer has a name' (line 27), but does this mean the name field is always populated, or can a customer exist temporarily without a name? If names are mandatory in the database, no constraint is needed. If they can be null/empty, this should be clarified.

source_references.excerpt: Yes, every customer has a name. It's just a text field.

ambiguities.description: Order status optionality is clear, but the effective date or transition logic is unaddressed. When does an order move from one status to the next? Are all status transitions valid, or are there rules (e.g., an order must be 'confirmed' before it can be 'shipped')? This should be clarified if status transitions are business-critical.

source_references.excerpt: Yes, an order has a status. The possible values are: pending, confirmed, shipped, and delivered.

ambiguities.description: The ternary fact 'Order contains Product with Quantity' includes a composite uniqueness constraint (each order-product combination appears once), but the minimum multiplicity of order lines is stated ('one or more products') without explicit maximum. Is there a business limit on the number of line items per order? The current model allows unlimited line items per order.

source_references.excerpt: An order contains one or more products. Each line in the order specifies a product and a quantity.

ambiguities.description: Billing system discrepancy: The transcript notes that the billing team defines 'clients' as customers who have 'actually paid' (line 31), but the CRM system has a broader definition. This implies a subtype relationship (PaidCustomer is a Customer) or a separate distinction rule. The current model treats 'Customer' and 'Client' as aliases, but if paid status is a distinct business concept, a separate fact type (Customer has PaidStatus) or subtype (PaidCustomer) may be warranted. Clarify whether 'PaidCustomer' is a distinct entity type or merely a filter view.

source_references.excerpt: One more thing -- I've heard some people call customers 'clients' in the billing system. Are those the same thing? Good question. In our CRM they're 'customers' but the billing team calls them 'clients.' For our purposes they're the same concept but the billing team has a slightly different definition -- they only consider someone a client once they've actually paid.
